# Submit It — and What You Built

One artifact. Five courses. Name every layer of it.

## The through-line

Nothing you built restarted. Each course added a layer to the same object.

**Course 1 — you signed something.** Your own transaction, built and sent from your own key, confirmed on devnet, and an account inspector that reads state back off the chain rather than off a screenshot. The first time the chain answered you specifically.

**Course 2 — the vault got a core.** Rust that models the vault's state and its rules, compiled green against the real toolchain on the build server. No local install, no version roulette.

**Course 3 — your program went live.** Deposit and withdraw, hardened, deployed to devnet. You own a program id, and a credential NFT that says you do.

**Course 4 — it became something other people can use.** A typed client generated from your own IDL, wrapped in an API you would actually import, published to npm with a semver policy you wrote down — and a deployed app at a public URL that installs that package from the registry and signs a real deposit through it.

**Course 5 — it started earning.** A Subscription Authority and a Recurring Delegation gave the app a paid tier that charges once per period and correctly refuses to charge twice. An x402 route returns a real 402 challenge naming the network, the asset and the payTo address. An agent calls that route on a loop, pays for each call out of a Fixed Delegation, and halts cleanly when the allowance says no.

Say the sentence out loud, because it is true and you will need it in a proposal:

> You started as a web2 JavaScript developer, and you now own a monetized on-chain product.

If you entered here — at C5 lesson 1, on the reference app, because you wanted payments and not Anchor — the same sentence applies to the payments layer you built. The credential still requires your own artifact, not the reference one.

## What is in scope, and what is not

The rails you learned are the ones open to you. From 2026-10-01, BCB Resolution 561 forbids a regulated eFX provider from taking reais, converting to a stablecoin, and settling the obligation abroad on-chain. That is a live constraint on a business model, not on you personally: individuals may still buy, sell, hold and transfer through authorized VASPs.

What this course built sits entirely inside what the resolution leaves open: **domestic merchant acceptance, contractor payouts, subscriptions, and agent budgets.** Every one of those is a real product surface, and every one of them is something an Earn listing has asked for. When you write a proposal, name the use case in those terms — a reviewer in Brazil reads the difference immediately, and it is a signal that you understand the market and not just the SDK.

## Pick a rail before you pick a package

The decision you now make without looking it up:

- **Fixed delegation** — a capped total that never refills. An allowance. This is what an autonomous agent holds, because the on-chain cap is what makes the autonomy safe.
- **Recurring delegation** — a cap that resets each period. Payroll, contractors, subscriptions. Skipped periods are lost.
- **Subscription plan** — a merchant publishes terms and approved pullers collect against them.
- **Solana Pay** — a human paying once, at a checkout. A decision, not an install: `@solana/pay@1.0.23` peer-depends on `@solana/kit ^6.9.0`, which does not admit the `@solana/kit@7.0.0` this course pins everywhere else.
- **x402** — stateless per-request metering. No delegation, no relationship, one call.

That list is the most portable thing you learned. Packages will move; the shape of the requirement will not.

## Submit one listing

Now the part most people skip.

**The calibration, honestly.** What this path realistically opens is **your first $500 to $5,000** of paid on-chain work. It is not a job offer, and anyone telling you a course makes you hireable as a Solana developer is selling something. The $5,000 frontend listing drew 731 submissions. The odds live somewhere else.

**Where they live.** Two termini this course specifically unlocks:

1. **Payments technical demos** — around $100 of reward per competitor, second only to Rust listings on that measure. You have a metered endpoint and a paid tier already running.
2. **Educational modules** — $2,500–$3,000, typically closing near 10 submissions. Your deep dive from the last lesson is most of one.

**How to read a listing, which is a skill in itself.** Competition is a function of **time-to-deadline**, not of category. The Zeroclaw listing sat at twelve submissions or fewer for most of its run and closed at 52 as the deadline approached. A submission count you read today tells you where that listing is in its life, not how contested it is. So: **never quote a single-day count as a competition rate.** Filter for **newly-opened development listings** and compare medians across listings that have actually closed.

**Then submit.** One listing, this week, with a real artifact attached. Not a plan to submit. The bar is lower than it looks — most listings are decided among a handful of complete, reproducible submissions, and you now have the two things most submissions lack: something that runs, and a write-up that says which versions it ran against.

## One more door

Turbin3 runs cohort-based Solana builder programs, and its prerequisites are the kind of thing C1–C4 already satisfy: your own deployed program, a published client, a deployed app. If you want structure and a cohort after this, that is where to look. Bring the program id and the package URL.

That is the course. Submit the listing.

blocks.prompt: Paste the URL of the Superteam Earn listing you submitted to, and the URL of what you submitted. Then, in three lines: which rail the work uses (fixed delegation, recurring delegation, subscription plan, Solana Pay or x402), which Brazilian use case it serves, and the one thing in your submission a reviewer can run themselves.

questions.prompt: A café in São Paulo wants a QR code on the counter so a customer can pay for one coffee in USDC from a phone wallet. No account, no relationship, no repeat. Which rail?

options.label: Solana Pay — a human paying once at a checkout
A recurring delegation, with a one-second period
options.feedback: A delegation is a standing approval between two known parties. A walk-in customer has no relationship to approve.

options.label: An x402 challenge returned from the till's API
options.feedback: x402 meters a machine calling an endpoint. There is no HTTP client here — there is a person with a phone.

options.label: A fixed delegation sized to the price of one coffee
options.feedback: You would be asking the customer to set up an on-chain allowance before their first sip. The setup cost exceeds the payment.

questions.explanation: Rail selection is the portable skill. One-off human checkout is Solana Pay's exact shape — and note it stays a decision, not an install, because @solana/pay@1.0.23 peer-depends on @solana/kit ^6.9.0 and will not sit in a kit 7 lockfile.

questions.prompt: From 2026-10-01, which of these does BCB Resolution 561 put off-limits?

options.label: A regulated eFX provider taking reais, converting to USDC, and settling the obligation abroad on-chain
A Brazilian merchant accepting USDC from a domestic customer
options.feedback: Domestic merchant acceptance is explicitly in scope, and is one of the four surfaces this course targets.

options.label: An individual buying and holding a stablecoin through an authorized VASP
options.feedback: Individuals may still buy, sell, hold and transfer via authorized VASPs. The resolution constrains a provider's business model, not a person's wallet.

options.label: Paying a Brazilian contractor in USDC on a recurring delegation
options.feedback: Contractor payouts are in scope. That is one of the reasons the recurring delegation matters in this market.

questions.explanation: Published 2026-04-30, effective 2026-10-01. In scope and legal for what you built: domestic merchant acceptance, contractor payouts, subscriptions, agent budgets.

questions.prompt: You are choosing the payment mint for a subscription product. Which statement is the decision rule you learned?

options.label: Legacy Token by default; Token-2022 only when a named extension is required — then verify your rail accepts it, because the Subscriptions program rejects any mint with a configured TransferHook
Token-2022 always, because it is the newer standard and legacy Token is being retired
options.feedback: Neither is being retired, and download volume is at parity (~1.27M/wk vs ~1.24M/wk). "Newer" is not a reason.

options.label: Legacy Token always, because Token-2022 has limited DEX support
options.feedback: That claim is stale — support is at parity now. The reason to prefer legacy is the absence of a requirement, not a compatibility gap.

options.label: Either one — the Subscriptions program treats both token programs identically
options.feedback: It supports both token programs, but it rejects a mint with a configured TransferHook. A Token-2022 mint is not automatically acceptable to your rail.

questions.explanation: Pick the extension you need, then check the rail. A TransferHook mint is the concrete case where a valid Token-2022 mint is refused.

questions.prompt: Why does the Subscriptions program put a program-controlled Subscription Authority between the user and every delegation, instead of approving each delegatee on the token account directly?

options.label: A token account can have only ONE approved delegate, so one wallet could never hold a subscription and an allowance and a merchant agreement on the same mint
PDAs are cheaper to create than token accounts
options.feedback: Rent is not the reason. The authority exists to lift a hard one-delegate limit.

options.label: It lets the program hold a keypair on the user's behalf
options.feedback: A PDA has no private key — that is the point of deriving it rather than generating it. Nothing holds a keypair for the user.

options.label: It is required in order to use Token-2022 mints
options.feedback: Unrelated. The authority is about delegate multiplicity, not about which token program owns the mint.

questions.explanation: One authority per (user, mint), derived with findSubscriptionAuthorityPda, and you branch on .exists before initialising — running init twice is the classic error.

questions.prompt: Fixed delegation versus recurring delegation. Which pair of statements is correct?

options.label: Fixed caps a total that never refills; recurring caps an amount that resets every period
Fixed caps an amount per period; recurring caps a lifetime total
options.feedback: Reversed. "Fixed" names a fixed total, not a fixed schedule.

options.label: Fixed is for Token-2022 mints; recurring is for legacy Token mints
options.feedback: Neither model is tied to a token program. The distinction is whether the cap refills.

options.label: Both refill; fixed refills daily and recurring refills on a period you choose
options.feedback: A fixed delegation never refills. That is exactly why it is the right budget for an autonomous agent.

questions.explanation: Capped total = an allowance = the agent's budget. Cap resets per period = payroll, contractors, subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A recurring delegation is set to 5 USDC per period. The delegatee collects nothing for one full period. What is the allowance at the start of the next period?

options.label: 5 USDC — the cap is restored, not increased
10 USDC — the skipped period carries forward
options.feedback: Nothing accumulates. A merchant who forgets to collect loses that period's revenue permanently.

options.label: 0 — a skipped period suspends the delegation until the user re-approves
options.feedback: Skipping costs revenue, not the delegation. Only expiryTs ends it.

options.label: 5 USDC, plus whatever was left unspent in the previous period
options.feedback: Unspent headroom is discarded on rollover. The cap is set back to amountPerPeriod, never added to.

questions.explanation: Rollover resets the cap. It is what bounds the delegatee's draw to one period at a time, and it is the semantic most write-ups get wrong.

questions.prompt: Your billing job runs twice by accident inside the same period. What does the second transferRecurring call do?

options.label: Fails with AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_PERIOD_LIMIT — no partial transfer occurs
Succeeds, and the excess is deducted from the next period
options.feedback: There is no borrowing across periods. The cap is enforced per period, at the moment of the call.

options.label: Transfers whatever remains of the period allowance and reports a partial fill
options.feedback: There is no partial fill. A pull for more than the remaining allowance is rejected outright — which is why a retry loop must treat this error as terminal for the period, not as transient.

options.label: Succeeds — the program deduplicates identical charges automatically
options.feedback: Nothing deduplicates for you. Idempotency is your job; the cap is the backstop.

questions.explanation: Handling this error correctly is the difference between a billing job that double-charges and one that does not. Treat it as "already collected this period."

questions.prompt: Across the whole delegation lifecycle, who signs what?

options.label: The user signs the setup — creating the authority and the delegation
The delegatee signs each transfer
The user signs the revoke, which closes the PDA and returns the rent to the signer or to the recorded receiver
The user must co-sign every transfer alongside the delegatee
options.feedback: That would reintroduce the per-charge signature the primitive exists to eliminate. The period cap is what bounds the delegatee, not a second signature.

questions.explanation: One approval, many collections, revocable at any time. That asymmetry is the security model of the whole module.

questions.prompt: A client hits your metered route with no payment. What does a valid x402 v2 challenge have to tell them, and who does the on-chain work?

options.label: An accepts[] envelope naming the network, the asset and the payTo address — and the facilitator does verify, settle and supported, so the API provider never touches on-chain infrastructure
A price in USD and a wallet address; the API server submits the transaction itself
options.feedback: A bare address does not say which chain or which asset, and running settlement in your API server is exactly what the facilitator exists to remove.

options.label: A signed transaction for the client to submit unchanged
options.feedback: The server states terms; the client constructs and signs the payment. It is a challenge, not a pre-built transaction.

options.label: Only a price — the client is expected to already know the network and asset from your docs
options.feedback: Then a generic client could never pay you. Self-description is the whole point of the envelope.

questions.explanation: Metering is a protocol, not a checkout page. The envelope is what lets a client that has never seen your API pay for one call.

questions.prompt: "@x402/svm" exports both ExactSvmScheme and ExactSvmSchemeV1. Why?

options.label: Both protocol versions are live on the wire, with different header names and different envelope fields, so a client has to detect which one a server speaks
V1 is a deprecated alias kept for backwards source compatibility; it behaves identically
options.feedback: They are not interchangeable. The header names and envelope fields differ, which is why you decide the version before you build the payment.

options.label: One is for devnet and one is for mainnet
options.feedback: Network selection is SOLANA_DEVNET_CAIP2 and friends, an entirely separate axis from protocol version.

options.label: One is for legacy Token and one is for Token-2022
options.feedback: Token program addresses are exported separately as TOKEN_PROGRAM_ADDRESS and TOKEN_2022_PROGRAM_ADDRESS. Not the same axis.

questions.explanation: Reading which version a server speaks, rather than assuming, is what keeps an integration alive. It is also why the scoped 2.19.0 packages and the frozen unscoped 1.2.0 packages must never be mixed.

questions.prompt: You fetch a metered URL and get a 402 with an empty response body. What is the correct next step?

options.label: Read the base64 envelope out of the PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header — some hosts ship no body at all
Treat it as a malformed response and retry the bare request
options.feedback: Retrying without paying returns the same 402 forever. This is the number one x402 integration failure and it is a parsing bug, not a server bug.

options.label: Fall back to the v1 scheme, since only v1 servers send empty bodies
options.feedback: Body placement and protocol version are independent. Decode the envelope first, then decide the version from its contents.

options.label: Pay a default amount to the address in your configuration
options.feedback: Never pay against a value the server did not state in this response. That is how a client overpays or pays the wrong asset.

questions.explanation: Envelope in the body or envelope in the header — handle both, then filter accepts[] on network and asset before you build anything.

questions.prompt: Your agent loop hits its spend limit mid-run. What should the correct implementation do, and what was the budget?

options.label: Halt and report — the budget was a Fixed Delegation drawn down with transferFixed, and the program refusing the next payment is the exit condition
Top the delegation up from the same signer and continue, since the agent is trusted
options.feedback: An agent that can raise its own cap has no cap. Refilling requires the user's signature by design.

options.label: Fall back to a raw keypair the agent holds so the run can complete
options.feedback: A raw keypair with unlimited funds is precisely what the on-chain cap replaces. That fallback deletes the safety property.

options.label: Retry with exponential backoff until the allowance recovers
options.feedback: A fixed delegation never refills. The retry loop would run forever.

questions.explanation: The exit condition is the learning objective. What makes agent autonomy safe is that the cap lives on-chain, where the agent cannot reach it.

questions.prompt: You are charging 5 USDC (6 decimals) through the Subscriptions client. Which amount argument is correct?

options.label: 5_000_000n — base units, as a bigint
5 — the client converts from display units for you
options.feedback: Nothing converts. Passing 5 charges five millionths of a dollar, succeeds, and goes unnoticed for weeks.

options.label: 5.0 — a float, since USDC has decimals
options.feedback: Amounts are integers in base units. A float cannot represent a token amount exactly and the API does not accept one.

options.label: "5000000" — a decimal string
options.feedback: Right magnitude, wrong type. These APIs take bigint, in the same way Kit takes Address rather than a PublicKey object.

questions.explanation: Base units as bigint, everywhere in this stack, on @solana/kit 7.0.0. The type is a habit worth having.

questions.prompt: Which two things must a deep dive on this material carry to stay verifiable a year from now?

options.label: A dated banner recording when you last ran the code
Exact package versions copied out of the lockfile that actually resolved
A screenshot of a successful transaction in the explorer
options.feedback: A screenshot proves it worked once, for you. It does not let a reader reproduce anything.

options.label: A caret range on each dependency so readers get bug fixes automatically
options.feedback: On a pre-1.0 package a caret admits breaking minors. That is the opposite of reproducible.

questions.explanation: Dated and pinned. Two paragraphs of work, and the reason your piece outlives every competing one.

questions.prompt: A listing you are considering shows 12 submissions today. What can you conclude?

options.label: Almost nothing — the count tracks time-to-deadline, so compare medians across listings that have already closed
It is under-contested; submit immediately for good odds
options.feedback: The Zeroclaw listing sat at twelve or fewer for most of its run and closed at 52. A mid-run count is not a competition rate.

options.label: The category is unpopular and probably low quality
options.feedback: Competition is a function of deadline proximity, not of category popularity.

options.label: It will close near 12, since submissions arrive at a steady rate
options.feedback: They do not arrive at a steady rate. Submissions cluster hard against the deadline.

questions.explanation: Filter for newly-opened development listings, and calibrate on closed ones. The realistic promise of this path is your first $500 to $5,000 of paid work.

questions.prompt: Seeded from the previous course. A wallet account advertises "solana:signAndSendTransaction". Which signer do you build, and who broadcasts?

options.label: createTransactionSendingSignerFromWalletAccount — the wallet broadcasts, and you never see the signed bytes
createTransactionSignerFromWalletAccount — your app broadcasts
options.feedback: That is the signer for the "solana:signTransaction" feature, which hands you signed bytes to send yourself.

options.label: createMessageSignerFromWalletAccount — the wallet broadcasts
options.feedback: Message signing does not produce a transaction, so nobody broadcasts anything.

options.label: Either transaction signer works; the feature list is advisory
options.feedback: It is not advisory — createSignerFromWalletAccount inspects the features at call time and throws when neither transaction feature exists.

questions.explanation: Feature to signer to who-broadcasts. Getting this wrong produces a transaction that is signed and never sent, or sent twice.

questions.prompt: Also seeded from the previous course. You are publishing the client package under a scope for the first time. What must be true, or the publish fails?

options.label: The first publish of a scoped package needs --access public, otherwise it 402s as a private package
NPM_TOKEN must be set as a repository secret
options.feedback: Trusted publishing via OIDC is the route taught — id-token write permission and a configured trusted publisher, no token. The token route is only the fallback.

options.label: The package version must be 1.0.0 or higher
options.feedback: npm accepts any valid semver, including 0.x. Nothing about the first publish requires 1.0.0.

options.label: The scope must match your GitHub organisation name
options.feedback: npm scopes and GitHub orgs are independent namespaces.

questions.explanation: The single most common first-publish failure, and the reason to pre-empt it rather than debug it in front of a bounty deadline.
